title: Alan Turing's Life In Reverse | From a Wilmslow Study to a London Nursery
description:
Alan Turing's life is told backwards in this episode, opening at his death in Wilmslow in 1954 and rewinding through the years after the war to his birth in west London in 1912. The journey steps through Manchester's first computers, the design of the stored program machine at Teddington, the naval codebreaking at Bletchley Park, and the 1936 paper that described the machine now named for him. Every scene moves to an earlier year, so the machines and the ideas appear in reverse order and the costs of his conviction become clear. Dates and places follow the documented record, and the accounts that dispute his death are named as disputed.

scenes.narration: In 2021 his face went onto the British fifty pound banknote, and Bletchley Park, the country house where he broke naval codes, is now a museum where visitors walk through his reconstructed machines. Engineers still use the term for his machine as a piece of standard vocabulary, and the question he asked in 1950 is still argued over.

Eight years before that, in 2013, the crown granted him a royal pardon for the conviction that had ended his public career. The pardon covered an offence that is no longer a crime, and Parliament later extended relief to thousands of men who had been convicted under the same law. The reversal came fifty-nine years after his death.

On June 7, 1954, Alan Turing was found dead at his home in Wilmslow, a village south of Manchester. He was forty-one years old. The coroner recorded a verdict of suicide by cyanide poisoning. Some later biographers have argued that the death may have been accidental, and the question has never been settled one way or the other.

Two years earlier, in July 1952, he had published a paper on how patterns form in living things, arguing that simple chemicals spreading through tissue could set out the stripes of a animal and the spiral of a shell. The paper came out in a scientific journal weeks after his trial. It is now one of the foundations of the study of growth.

Five months before that, in January 1952, the police had come to his house in Cheshire after he reported a burglary. They found evidence of a relationship with a man, which was then a criminal offence, and he was charged. He did not deny it. In March he was convicted and chose a course of hormone treatment in place of prison, and his security work was taken away.

Two years before that, in October 1950, the journal Mind had printed his paper asking whether a machine could think. He proposed replacing the question with a test in which a machine and a person answer written questions, and the judge decides which is which. He predicted that by the end of the century the machines would fool most questioners.

Seven years earlier, in 1948, he had moved to Manchester University as deputy director of the laboratory that ran the Ferranti Mark I, one of the first computers built for sale. He wrote the instruction manual for it, which became one of the first textbooks on how to program a machine. He was thirty-five, and the machine filled a room.

A year before that, in 1947, he had finished the design of an electronic machine at the National Physical Laboratory near London. It used valves and a stored program, and it was built later as a smaller machine called the Pilot ACE, which ran in 1950 after he had already left for Manchester. The design was the work of one mind.

In 1946 he was appointed an officer of the Order of the British Empire for the codebreaking work of the war. The work itself was still secret. The public history of the period did not mention Bletchley Park for decades, and he could not put the most important years of his life on his own papers or in his lectures.

The year before that, in 1945, he had joined the National Physical Laboratory at Teddington as an assistant director and set about drawing up a complete design for a computing engine. It was one of the first full descriptions of a stored program machine anywhere. He worked with a small group of engineers and wrote to them in clear, plain sentences.

In May 1945 the war in Europe ended, and the work that had filled six years at the country house came to a close. The codebreakers were told to keep quiet, and most of them returned to universities and firms as if the previous years had been ordinary. He had learned how large teams of people could be organized around a machine.

Two years earlier, between 1943 and 1944, he had built a device to scramble speech for telephone calls, working with a young engineer at a signals establishment in Buckinghamshire. The system, which they called Delilah, scrambled a voice into noise and rebuilt it at the other end. It worked on the test bench, but the war was nearly over and it was never used in service.

Through 1942 and into 1943 his unit was blocked by a new naval cipher with an extra rotor, and the messages they had read for months went dark. When the method was recovered, the reading of those messages resumed, and shipping losses changed. He had also travelled to Washington in 1941 to work alongside American naval codebreakers, so the two services shared the load.

Two years earlier, in October 1941, he had sailed for the United States to work with the American navy on its version of the German naval cipher. He stayed for some months, taking part in meetings in Washington and returning with a clearer picture of how the two countries would divide the work. The Atlantic convoys depended on what they found.

In June 1941, after a year of work in a wooden hut, his group began reading the German naval messages again, which gave the convoy escorts the positions of the submarines hunting them. It was the hardest of the daily codes and the one that mattered most to Britain's supply of food and fuel. The work was done with machines he had helped design.

Through 1940 and 1941 he had also worked out a statistical shortcut for narrowing naval cipher settings, using long paper strips printed with letter patterns. The method, which he named Banburismus after the town where the strips were printed, cut the work of the day considerably. He kept notes on it, and the technique outlived the war in the notebooks he left.

In March 1940 the first of his electromechanical machines, known as the Bombe, started running, using rotating drums to test the possible settings of the German Enigma machine at speed. A colleague added an improvement that cut the number of steps again. The machines were built in banks by engineers in London and at a factory in Britain, and they worked day and night.

Seven months earlier, on September 4, 1939, the day after war was declared, he had reported to a country house in Buckinghamshire that had been taken over as a codebreaking station. He arrived with a bicycle and a rucksack, and was put in charge of the group working on the naval version of the German cipher.

Two years earlier, in 1938, he had taken his doctorate at Princeton University in New Jersey under a logician who had formalized the idea of computation, and then returned to his fellowship at King's College in Cambridge. His thesis was about a system of logic built on the order of numbers. He could have stayed in America, and he chose to go home.

Two years before that, in the autumn of 1936, he had crossed the Atlantic to Princeton as a young graduate. He had been at Cambridge for five years and had already produced the paper that made his name. The department there was small, and he worked through the summer on problems of his own choosing.

Earlier in that year, before he left, he had finished the paper that answered a challenge set by mathematicians about what can be decided by proof. He described an abstract machine reading and writing symbols on a tape, and showed that one such machine could imitate any other given the right description. The idea gave computers their basic shape before any computer existed.

In 1935 he had been made a Fellow of King's College, Cambridge, for work in probability, at the age of twenty-two. The fellowship gave him rooms, a small income and a place among the college's mathematicians. He now had the standing to publish and to teach, and he used it to follow questions that his tutors had not set him.

A year before that, in 1934, he had finished his degree at King's College with first class honours in mathematics. He had arrived three years earlier, in 1931, and had thrown himself into the life of the college, its lectures, its rowing and its long arguments. The course was formal and classical, and he was already working beyond it.

Three years before that, in 1931, he had gone up to King's College, Cambridge, at nineteen. The place was small, liberal and full of mathematicians who argued about everything. He had been pushed hard at school for the classics, and here the mathematics he had been doing on his own turned out to be the ordinary language of the room.

A year earlier, in 1930, his closest friend at school had died suddenly of an illness at the age of eighteen. Alan was seventeen, and the two of them had exchanged letters about chemistry, experiments and the nature of the mind. He kept the letters, and later wrote to the friend's mother about what he thought had happened. He never forgot the year.

In September 1926, at thirteen, he had gone away to a public school in Dorset where the timetable was built around Latin, Greek and the ancient historians. The masters told his parents that he would do better if he concentrated on the classics. He kept his science, won prizes in it, and read ahead of the class in mathematics.

Through the years before that he and his brother had lived in England while their father's work kept the family in India, and they were looked after by a couple on the south coast. They saw their parents only on leave. He was a quiet boy who preferred machines and chemical experiments to the games that the school expected him to play.

He was born on June 23, 1912, in Maida Vale, a district of west London, to Julius and Ethel Turing. His father worked for the government in India, so the household moved between two countries, and the boys were sent to England to be schooled. The child was called Alan, and he grew up with a brother three years older.
